courses.title: Electrician basics — safety first
courses.summary: Understand how electricity reaches and moves through an Indian home, how MCBs, RCCBs and earthing protect you, what the wire colours mean, and the safe-isolation routine every electrician follows before touching anything.
outcomes: Learners can explain volts, amps, watts and units (kWh) with home examples
Learners can describe and follow the safe-isolation routine: switch off, lock and tag, test dead
Learners can tell what an MCB, an RCCB and earthing each protect against
Learners can identify Indian wiring colours and socket ratings, and know never to trust colour alone
Learners can respond correctly to an electric-shock emergency

lessons.title: How electricity works in your home

story.title: Arjun's first day at the workshop

scenes.text: Arjun, 19, joins Rafiq bhai's electrical shop in Indore as a helper. On day one Rafiq bhai hands him a tester and says: 'First you understand. Then you touch.'
They visit a flat where the geyser keeps tripping the switch. The owner asks, 'Why can't you just put a bigger fuse?'
Rafiq bhai does a quick sum on a scrap of paper: watts ÷ volts = amps. 'The wire decides the fuse. Not the customer,' he says.
Arjun realises electricity is not magic — it is numbers, and the numbers keep people alive.

steps.title: Voltage, current and power — in plain words
steps.body:
Think of electricity like water in a pipe.

- **Voltage (V)** is the push, like water pressure. Indian homes get about **230 V single-phase AC at 50 Hz**. Bigger buildings and some homes take **three-phase supply (about 400–415 V between phases)**.
- **Current (A, amperes)** is how much electricity flows, like litres per second.
- **Power (W, watts)** is how fast energy is used. **Power = Voltage × Current** (P = V × I).
- **Resistance (Ω, ohms)** opposes flow. Ohm's law: **V = I × R**.

A 230 V supply is enough to stop a human heart. A current of only tens of milliamps through the chest can be fatal. That is why every step in this course starts with safety.

steps.title: Worked example: how many amps does a geyser draw?
steps.body:
A geyser is rated **2000 W**. Supply is **230 V**.

I = P ÷ V = 2000 ÷ 230 ≈ **8.7 A**.

So it must go on a circuit and socket rated well above 8.7 A — in India that means a **16 A socket** on a suitably sized wire and breaker, not a small 6 A socket.

Now you try: a 1000 W iron → 1000 ÷ 230 ≈ 4.3 A. A 60 W fan → about 0.26 A.

steps.title: What is a 'unit' on your electricity bill?
steps.body:
One **unit = 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh)** = using 1000 W for 1 hour.

- 2000 W geyser for 30 minutes = 2 kW × 0.5 h = **1 unit**
- 10 LED bulbs of 9 W for 5 hours = 90 W × 5 h = 450 Wh = **0.45 unit**
- A 1.5-ton AC can draw roughly 1.2–1.8 kW depending on model and star rating — so a few hours a day adds many units.

Multiplying units by your tariff (₹ per unit, set by your state's electricity regulator) gives the energy charge.

steps.title: Phase, neutral and earth
steps.body:
A home circuit has three conductors:

- **Phase (live / line)**: carries the 230 V. This is the dangerous one.
- **Neutral**: the return path. It is close to earth potential *in normal conditions*, but it can carry current and can become dangerous if there is a fault — never treat neutral as safe.
- **Earth**: a safety path to the ground (via an earth pit or the supply earth). It normally carries no current; it carries fault current so that protection devices trip.

Switches must always break the **phase**, never only the neutral. A switch on the neutral leaves the bulb holder live even when 'off'.

steps.title: Common mistakes beginners make
steps.body:
- 'It's only 230 volts' — 230 V kills people every year in India.
- 'The switch is off so it's safe' — the switch might be on the neutral, or the circuit may be fed from elsewhere.
- Replacing a tripping breaker with a bigger one — the breaker protects the **wire**; upsizing it lets the wire overheat and start a fire.
- Wet hands, bare feet, metal ladders — each one lowers your body's resistance.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Look at the rating sticker on three appliances at home (fan, fridge, mixer). Write the watts. Calculate the amps (W ÷ 230) and the units used per day for your family's typical use. Compare with your bill.

activity.prompt: A 1500 W induction cooktop runs on 230 V. About how many amperes does it draw? (Round to 1 decimal)

quiz.q: What is the normal single-phase supply voltage in Indian homes?
quiz.why: India's standard single-phase supply is about 230 V AC at 50 Hz.

quiz.q: A 2000 W appliance used for 2 hours consumes how many units?
Which conductor should a light switch break?
quiz.why: Switching the phase makes the fitting dead when off. Switching only neutral leaves it live.

quiz.q: Why should you never fit a bigger breaker because one keeps tripping?
options: The breaker protects the wire; a bigger one lets the wire overheat
It is illegal to buy one
quiz.why: Breakers are sized to the wire. Oversizing removes protection and risks fire.

lessons.title: Never work live: the safe-isolation routine

scenes.text: In Lucknow, Sunil was changing a switch board. He touched it with his neon tester screwdriver — no glow. He started unscrewing.
A spark jumped. Sunil was lucky: a small burn and a bad fright. The board was fed from a second circuit, and his tester's bulb was weak.
His instructor, Kavita ma'am, made the whole batch learn one routine: isolate, lock, tag, prove, test, prove.
'A tester that shows nothing has not proved anything,' she said. 'You must prove the tester works before and after.'

steps.title: Rule one: never work on live circuits
steps.body:
Electricity can kill. This course teaches understanding and safe habits; it does not make you a licensed electrician. Work on building wiring should be done by, or under the supervision of, a licensed electrician as required by your state's electrical licensing rules.

Professional electricians assume **every wire is live until they have proved it dead** with a proper tester. Live working is a specialist activity done only by trained, authorised people with insulated tools and PPE — it is not something a learner, helper or homeowner does.

steps.title: The safe-isolation routine (learn it in order)
steps.body:
1. **Identify** the circuit you will work on (check the labelled distribution board).
2. **Switch off** the correct MCB — or the main switch if unsure.
3. **Lock and tag**: lock the breaker off if a lock-off device is available, and hang a tag: 'Do not switch on — work in progress — name, phone'. Tell everyone in the house.
4. **Prove your tester** on a known live source (a socket you know is on).
5. **Test dead**: test between phase–neutral, phase–earth and neutral–earth at the point of work.
6. **Prove your tester again** on the known live source — this confirms it did not fail during the test.
7. Only now start work. If anything is unclear, stop and ask.

steps.title: Why the neon tester screwdriver is not enough
steps.body: The cheap neon screwdriver tester is useful for a quick hint, but it is **not proof**: it depends on your body as part of the path, may not glow in bright light, can fail silently, and does not test between phase and neutral. Use a **two-pole voltage tester or a multimeter in the correct AC voltage range** for proving dead, and still follow the prove–test–prove routine.

steps.title: Basic PPE and habits
steps.body:
- Dry hands, dry floor; rubber-soled shoes.
- Insulated tools in good condition (no cracked handles).
- Wooden or fibreglass ladder — never aluminium near wiring.
- Remove rings, watches and metal chains.
- One-hand rule while testing where possible, to avoid current across the chest.
- Never work alone on anything bigger than a simple fitting.

steps.title: If someone gets an electric shock
steps.body:
1. **Do not touch them** while they may still be in contact with the supply.
2. **Switch off** at the MCB / main switch or pull the plug.
3. If you cannot switch off, push the source away with a **dry non-conducting object** (dry wood, plastic) while standing on something dry.
4. Call **112**.
5. If they are not breathing normally, start **CPR** and continue until help arrives. Cool burns with cool running water.
6. Anyone who has had a significant shock should be checked by a doctor — heart rhythm problems can appear later.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Without opening anything, walk to your home's distribution board. Find the main switch and the MCBs. Are they labelled? Write a simple label list (e.g. 'MCB 3 — kitchen sockets') with an adult or the house owner.

activity.prompt: Put the safe-isolation routine in the correct order.
items: Identify the circuit on the distribution board
Switch off the correct MCB
Lock off and tag the breaker
Prove the tester on a known live source
Test the circuit dead at the point of work

quiz.q: Your tester shows no voltage on a circuit. What must you do before trusting it?
options: Prove the tester on a known live source before and after
Switch the MCB on and off quickly
quiz.why: A failed tester also shows nothing. Prove–test–prove confirms the result.

quiz.q: Why hang a tag on the switched-off breaker?
options: So no one switches it on while you work
It is needed for the bill
quiz.why: Tags and locks stop someone restoring power while you are working.

quiz.q: Someone is stuck to a live wire. First action?
options: Switch off the supply or push the source away with dry wood
Wait for them to let go
quiz.why: Never touch them directly; cut the supply or separate them using a dry non-conductor.

quiz.q: Which ladder is safest near electrical work?
quiz.why: Non-conducting ladders reduce the risk of a current path through you.

quiz.q: Which number should you call in India for an emergency?
quiz.why: 112 is India's all-emergency number. (1098 is Childline; 14416 is Tele-MANAS.)

lessons.title: Your distribution board: MCB, RCCB and earthing

scenes.text: In Kochi, Mrs. Thomas's power went off every time it rained. She called electrician Biju.
Biju opened only the outer cover of the board and pointed: 'This is your RCCB. It tripped because current is leaking somewhere — probably water in the outdoor light.'
He isolated the circuit, found water inside the garden lamp, dried it, replaced the gasket and fitted a weatherproof fitting.
'Never remove the RCCB because it trips,' he told her. 'It just told you about a leak that could have killed someone.'

steps.title: What lives in a distribution board (DB)
steps.body:
From the meter, supply goes to your **DB**. Typically you will see:

- A **main switch / isolator** (switches off everything).
- An **RCCB** (or several) — protects people against leakage/earth-fault current.
- Several **MCBs**, one per circuit (lights, sockets, AC, geyser, kitchen).
- **Neutral and earth bars** behind the cover.

Only the switch handles and test button are meant for the user. Opening the inner cover exposes live parts — that is a job for a licensed electrician.

steps.title: MCB — protects the wire
steps.body:
A **Miniature Circuit Breaker** trips on:

- **Overload** — too much current for too long (e.g. three heaters on one circuit). A heat-sensitive (thermal) part trips it.
- **Short circuit** — phase touching neutral/earth, huge current instantly. A magnetic part trips it in a fraction of a second.

Common ratings: 6 A, 10 A, 16 A, 20 A, 32 A. 'B' curve MCBs are common for homes; 'C' curve tolerate higher starting currents (motors, ACs). The rating is chosen to match the **wire size**, so the wire never overheats.

**An MCB does not protect you from electric shock** — a shock current of a few tens of milliamps is far too small to trip a 16 A breaker.

steps.title: RCCB — protects people
steps.body:
A **Residual Current Circuit Breaker** compares the current going out on phase with the current returning on neutral. If they differ — meaning some current is leaking to earth, perhaps through a person — it trips.

- **30 mA** RCCBs are used for protection of people.
- 100 mA / 300 mA types are used mainly for fire protection.
- An RCCB alone does **not** protect against overload or short circuit — it is used together with MCBs (or as an **RCBO**, which combines both).
- Press the **'T' test button** regularly (e.g. monthly) — it should trip. If it does not, call an electrician.

steps.title: Earthing
steps.body:
The earth wire connects metal bodies of appliances (geyser, fridge, washing machine, iron) to the ground. If a live wire touches the metal body, fault current flows to earth and the MCB/RCCB trips, instead of the metal staying live waiting for someone to touch it.

Bad signs: tingling from a washing machine, sparks from a tap, a metal body that 'bites'. These mean an earth or insulation fault — stop using the appliance and call an electrician. Earth pits need periodic checking, especially in dry areas.

steps.title: Dangerous 'fixes' you must refuse
steps.body:
- Bypassing or removing an RCCB because it 'trips too much'.
- Wrapping wire around a fuse or using a thicker fuse wire.
- Using a two-pin plug for an appliance that needs earth.
- Joining earth to neutral to stop tripping.

Each of these turns a safety device off and leaves a hidden killer behind.

steps.title: Worked example: which device tripped and why?
steps.body:
- **Geyser circuit MCB (16 A) trips after 10 minutes, wire warm** → overload or loose connection heating up. Check load and connections (licensed electrician).
- **MCB trips instantly with a bang when you switch on a fan** → short circuit in the fan or wiring.
- **RCCB trips when washing machine runs, MCB fine** → leakage to earth in the machine (e.g. heater element or wet wiring).

Reading which device tripped is the first diagnostic clue.

activity.prompt: Which device mainly protects against each problem?

items.text: Too many heaters on one circuit
Current leaking through a person to earth
Wet outdoor lamp leaking to earth
Faulty washing machine body becoming live

quiz.q: What trip current is typical for an RCCB that protects people?
quiz.why: 30 mA RCCBs are used for personal protection.

quiz.q: Does a 16 A MCB protect you from electric shock?
options: No — shock currents are far too small to trip it
quiz.why: Shock currents of tens of milliamps cannot trip a 16 A MCB; that is the RCCB's job.

quiz.q: The RCCB test button should be pressed…
options: Regularly, e.g. monthly — it should trip
quiz.why: Regular testing confirms the mechanism works.

quiz.q: A washing machine gives a mild tingle. What does it suggest?
options: Earth or insulation fault — stop using it
quiz.why: Tingling metal means a fault; unplug and have it repaired.

quiz.q: An RCBO is…
options: A device combining RCCB and MCB functions
quiz.why: RCBO = residual current breaker with overcurrent protection.

lessons.title: Wires, colours and sockets in India

scenes.text: Priya, an electrical diploma student in Pune, visits two buildings. In the old one, phase is red, neutral black, earth green.
In the new flat, she sees brown, blue and green-yellow, like on imported appliances.
'Which one is correct?' she asks her mentor, Mr. Deshpande.
'You will meet both,' he says. 'Learn both — and then test, because someone may have used any colour they had.'

steps.title: Wiring colours you will meet in India
steps.body:
**Traditional Indian practice** (very common in existing buildings):

- Phase: **red** (in three-phase: **red, yellow, blue** for the three phases)
- Neutral: **black**
- Earth: **green** (or green with yellow stripe)

**International (harmonised) colours**, seen on most appliance cords and in many newer installations:

- Live/phase: **brown** (three-phase: brown, black, grey)
- Neutral: **blue**
- Earth: **green-and-yellow**

Notice the trap: **black is neutral in the old scheme but can be a phase in the new three-phase scheme**. Colours are a guide, never proof. **Always test.**

steps.title: Wire sizes (copper) — common practice
steps.body:
Wire size is the cross-section area in square millimetres (sq mm). Common practice in Indian homes:

- **1.0–1.5 sq mm**: lighting and fan points
- **2.5 sq mm**: 6 A socket circuits
- **4 sq mm**: 16 A power sockets — geyser, AC, oven (larger ACs or long runs may need more)
- **6 sq mm and above**: main incoming lines, depending on load

Exact sizes depend on length, load, how many wires share a conduit, and the applicable standards — a licensed electrician calculates them. Use ISI-marked wire from reputable makers; fake 'lightweight' wire with less copper is a known fire risk.

steps.title: Sockets and plugs
steps.body:
Indian homes mainly use round-pin three-pin sockets:

- **6 A sockets (smaller)** — phone chargers, TVs, laptops, fans, lamps.
- **16 A sockets (larger)** — geysers, ACs, room heaters, microwave ovens, washing machines.

The top (thicker) pin is **earth**. Use the right size plug; never force a 16 A appliance into a 6 A socket with an adapter, and never run heaters from extension boards or multi-plug adapters. Modular switches with shutters are safer for homes with children.

steps.title: Mistakes that start fires
steps.body:
- Twisting wires together and wrapping with tape instead of using proper connectors/terminals.
- Overloaded extension boards ('octopus' sockets).
- Loose terminal screws — they arc and heat up; look for brown/black marks.
- Thin wire feeding a heavy load.
- Using any colour wire 'because that's what was in the bag'.

steps.title: Try this (no tools needed)
steps.body: Look at the plug of a geyser or AC and a phone charger at home. Which socket size does each use? Look at an appliance cord where the outer sheath is cut back at the plug: can you see brown, blue and green-yellow? Note anything with burn marks or a warm plug — tell an adult.

activity.prompt: Match each wire or item with its meaning.

quiz.q: In the harmonised scheme, blue is…
quiz.why: Brown is live, blue is neutral, green-yellow is earth.

quiz.q: In traditional Indian wiring, earth is usually…
quiz.why: Earth has been green; green-yellow is now common.

quiz.q: Why can't you rely on colours alone?
options: Different schemes and past mistakes mean a wire may not be what its colour suggests
quiz.why: Old and new schemes mix, and installers make errors. Always test.

quiz.q: Which socket suits a 2 kW geyser?
quiz.why: About 8.7 A needs a 16 A socket on a suitable circuit.

quiz.q: Which pin is earth in an Indian three-pin plug?
quiz.why: The larger top pin is earth.

sources: IS 732 (code of practice for electrical wiring installations) — general awareness
IEC 60445 (identification of conductors)

lessons.title: Simple jobs, fault-finding and your career path

scenes.text: Meena, 22, has finished her ITI Electrician course in Jaipur and works with a contractor. Her first solo call: 'Fan not working, regulator hot.'
She switches off the MCB, tags it, proves her tester, tests dead — and only then opens the switchboard.
A loose, blackened terminal on the regulator. She replaces the regulator, tightens terminals properly and restores power.
She explains to the customer what happened and why loose connections are dangerous. The customer books her again for the whole flat.

steps.title: A fault-finding mindset
steps.body:
Professionals diagnose before they replace.

1. **Ask**: what happened, when, any smell, sound, or trip?
2. **Look** (with power off): burn marks, melted plastic, loose wires.
3. **Check the simple things first**: is the MCB on? Is the bulb fine? Is the regulator working?
4. **Isolate and test** using the safe-isolation routine.
5. **Fix the cause**, not just the symptom (e.g. replace a burnt terminal, don't just change the bulb).
6. **Test after repair** and explain to the customer.

steps.title: Worked example: replacing a bulb holder (supervised practice)
steps.body:
Under supervision, after isolation and testing dead:

- Note which wire goes where (take a photo).
- Loosen terminal screws, remove old holder.
- Strip insulation only as much as the terminal needs — no bare copper outside the terminal.
- Phase to the centre contact (for an Edison screw holder), neutral to the outer shell.
- Tighten firmly, tug-test each wire, refit cover.
- Restore power, test, remove your tag.

If any wire is brittle, burnt or the box is damaged — stop and report it.

steps.title: Training and licensing paths
steps.body:
- **ITI Electrician** trade (two years) is a common route; there are also short-term skill courses under national skilling schemes.
- Polytechnic **Diploma in Electrical Engineering** and B.Tech/BE go further into design.
- To do wiring work, electricians obtain a **wireman/electrician permit or supervisor certificate** and contractors a **contractor licence** from the state electrical licensing authority. Requirements differ by state — check your state's licensing board.
- Careers: house wiring, industrial maintenance, solar PV installation, panel wiring, lift and HVAC electrical, facility management.

steps.title: Professional habits customers remember
steps.body:
- Arrive on time, wear clean clothes, carry shoe covers.
- Give a clear estimate before starting; explain extra charges before doing extra work.
- Never leave exposed wires, and clean up.
- Refuse unsafe requests politely (bypassing an RCCB, oversizing a breaker) and explain why.
- Keep a simple job record: date, address, work done, materials, payment.

steps.title: Know when to say no
steps.body:
As a learner or helper, do not attempt: work inside the distribution board, meter-side connections (these belong to the electricity distribution company), three-phase work, anything near overhead lines, or any job you cannot isolate. Saying 'I will bring my senior' is professional, not weak.

This is general education, not a licence or a substitute for formal training.

a.text: A customer says: 'The MCB for the kitchen keeps tripping. Just put a 32 A one, I'll pay extra.' The kitchen circuit has 2.5 sq mm wire.

choices.label: Fit the 32 A MCB — customer is king
choices.feedback: This removes protection: 2.5 sq mm wire can overheat long before 32 A trips.

choices.label: Explain the risk and offer to find the cause of tripping
choices.feedback: Right — the breaker protects the wire. Find out why it trips.

b.text: You isolate the circuit and check. The customer runs a 2 kW induction, a microwave and an electric kettle together on one extension board.

choices.label: Suggest a separate 16 A circuit with proper wire for heavy appliances
choices.feedback: Excellent — the real fix is redistributing the load with proper wiring.

choices.label: Tell them to keep using the extension board but more carefully
choices.feedback: Heavy loads on extension boards are a fire risk; this does not fix the cause.

bad1.text: Months later the wire insulation inside the wall cooks and smokes. Oversizing the breaker hid the overload. The breaker must match the wire.

bad2.text: The extension board melts one evening. Luckily no one is hurt. Fix overload by redistributing load on properly sized circuits.

good.text: You give a written estimate for a new dedicated circuit, the customer agrees, and the tripping stops. You kept them safe and earned their trust.

quiz.q: What should you do FIRST on a service call about a hot regulator?
options: Ask questions, then isolate and test dead before opening
quiz.why: Gather information, then follow safe isolation.

quiz.q: In an Edison screw bulb holder, phase should connect to…
quiz.why: Phase to the centre contact reduces the chance of touching live metal when changing bulbs.

quiz.q: Who usually issues electrician permits and contractor licences in India?
quiz.why: Licensing is handled at state level; rules vary.

quiz.q: A customer asks you to bypass the RCCB. You should…
options: Refuse politely and explain it protects lives
quiz.why: Professionals refuse unsafe work and explain why.

quiz.q: Which job is NOT for a learner/helper?
quiz.why: Meter-side work belongs to the distribution company and trained staff.

options: Use a dry wooden stick to push the cable away while standing on a dry surface

options: Dangerous shock currents (tens of mA) are far below its trip current

options: It hides leakage, can make metal parts live and defeats the RCCB

courses.title: Plumbing basics for homes
courses.summary: How water comes in and goes out of an Indian home, which pipes are used where, how to fix a dripping tap and a blocked drain, and how to work as a trusted plumber.
outcomes: Learners can trace supply and drainage in a typical Indian house or flat
Learners can choose the right pipe material (CPVC, uPVC, PVC/SWR, GI, PPR) for a job
Learners can fix a dripping tap and seal threads correctly with PTFE tape
Learners can clear a blocked drain safely and explain why traps matter
Learners can estimate and quote a small plumbing job

lessons.title: How water moves through a home

scenes.text: Lakshmi runs a small paying-guest house in Hyderabad. Every summer the top-floor taps have poor flow.
Plumber Ramesh climbs to the terrace: a municipal line fills an underground sump, a pump lifts water to the overhead tank, and gravity brings it down.
'Your overhead tank is only a little higher than your top-floor shower,' he explains. 'Height gives pressure. Here there is almost none.'
He suggests a small booster pump for the top floor only. Lakshmi finally understands her own building.

steps.title: Two systems: supply and drainage
steps.body:
Every building has **two separate systems** that must never mix:

- **Supply (clean water)**: municipal line or borewell → often an **underground sump** → **pump** → **overhead tank** → down-take pipes → taps, geyser, flush tank. It is under pressure (from height or a pump).
- **Drainage (waste)**: from fixtures → traps → waste/soil pipes → inspection chambers → sewer or septic tank. It works by **gravity**, so pipes need a steady downward slope.

Grey water (basins, showers, washing) and black water (toilets) may run in separate stacks in larger buildings.

steps.title: Pressure from height
steps.body:
Each **10 metres** of water height gives about **1 bar** (≈ 1 kg/cm²) of pressure. A tank only 2 m above a shower gives roughly 0.2 bar — a weak trickle. Many modern mixers and instant geysers need more pressure than that, which is why top floors often add a **pressure pump**.

Worked example: tank base at 12 m, ground-floor tap at 1 m → height difference 11 m → about 1.1 bar at the tap (minus losses in the pipes).

steps.title: Pipe materials and where they go
steps.body:
- **CPVC**: hot and cold water supply inside homes; very common today; solvent-cement joints.
- **uPVC**: cold water supply only (not for hot water).
- **PPR**: hot and cold supply; joined by heat fusion with a special machine.
- **GI (galvanised iron)**: older buildings; threaded joints; rusts inside over years, reducing flow and colouring water.
- **PVC / SWR pipes**: drainage — soil, waste and rainwater; larger diameters (e.g. 75 mm, 110 mm).
- **HDPE**: underground/outdoor supply lines and borewells.

Common mistake: using uPVC on the geyser outlet — it softens and fails with hot water.

steps.title: Hygiene and safety basics
steps.body:
- Never allow a drainage pipe to connect into a supply pipe or tank — contamination spreads disease.
- Overhead tanks need a tight lid, an overflow pipe with a mesh, and regular cleaning (commonly every 6 months).
- Turn off the electric **pump and geyser** before working on their pipes; geyser water can scald.
- Wear gloves when dealing with drains; wash hands after.

steps.title: Try this

story.title: The drip that wasted thousands of litres

scenes.text: In Chennai, Mr. Iyer's kitchen tap dripped day and night. 'Only a drop,' he said.
His granddaughter Nila measured: a cup (about 200 ml) every 10 minutes. That is over 28 litres a day.
Plumber Selvi shut the isolation valve, opened the tap and replaced a worn rubber washer in 15 minutes.
Nila calculated the water saved in a year — over 10,000 litres. Mr. Iyer started checking all taps every month.

steps.title: Why taps drip
steps.body:
- **Washer-type (compression) taps**: a rubber washer presses on a seat. When the washer wears or hardens, water seeps past → drip from the spout.
- **Quarter-turn / ceramic disc taps**: two ceramic discs. Grit or a cracked disc cartridge causes drips; you replace the cartridge.
- **Leak from the spindle/handle** (not the spout) → worn gland packing or O-ring.

Always identify which type you have before buying parts — take the old part to the shop.

steps.title: Worked example: replacing a tap washer
steps.body:
1. Close the **angle valve / isolation valve** (or main valve). Open the tap fully to drain.
2. Put a cloth in the basin so small parts don't fall down the drain.
3. Remove the handle cap and screw; unscrew the headgear with a spanner (protect chrome with a cloth).
4. Remove the old washer; fit a new one of the same size.
5. Check the seat for damage; reassemble; open valve slowly; check for drips.

Common mistakes: forgetting to close the valve, over-tightening (crushes the new washer), scratching chrome with a bare wrench.

steps.title: PTFE (thread seal) tape — the right way
steps.body:
Thread tape seals the tiny gaps in threaded joints.

- Wrap it **in the same direction the fitting tightens** — clockwise when you look at the end of the male thread. Wrapped backwards, it unwinds as you screw in.
- Typically **3–5 wraps**, keeping it flat and starting one thread back from the end so tape doesn't enter the pipe.
- Do not use tape on joints that seal with a rubber washer or O-ring (like flexible connectors) — the washer does the sealing.
- Hand-tight plus a little more with a spanner; plastic fittings crack if forced.

steps.title: Finding hidden leaks
steps.body:
- **Meter test**: close all taps, note the water meter reading, wait an hour; if it moves, there is a leak.
- **Toilet cistern test**: a few drops of food colour in the cistern; if colour appears in the pan without flushing, the flapper/valve leaks.
- **Damp patches, peeling paint, fungus** on walls often trace back to concealed pipe joints or bathroom floor waterproofing failures.

steps.title: What a trap does
steps.body:
A **trap** (P-trap, S-trap, bottle trap, floor trap/Nahani trap) is a bend that always holds a little water — the **water seal**. This seal blocks foul gases and insects from coming up the drain.

Seals are lost by: drying out (unused fixtures), siphoning (poor venting), or cracks. Fix: refill with water; for repeated loss, check venting and the trap itself.

steps.title: Clearing a blocked drain — safely, in order
steps.body:
1. **Remove what you can see**: hair from the floor trap grating, food from the sink strainer.
2. **Plunger**: cover the overflow hole with a wet cloth, ensure some water in the basin, plunge firmly 10–15 times.
3. **Open the bottle trap** under the basin (bucket underneath) and clean it.
4. **Drain auger / snake** for deeper blockages.
5. Hot (not boiling, for PVC) water helps with grease in kitchen sinks.

Never **mix chemical drain cleaners** with each other or with bleach/acid — toxic gas and burns can result. If you use one, follow the label, wear gloves and eye protection, and never plunge after adding chemicals (splash risk).

steps.title: Slope matters
steps.body: Horizontal drainage pipes need a steady fall. A common rule of thumb for small-diameter waste pipes is about **1 in 40 to 1 in 60** (e.g. 2.5 cm drop for each 1–1.5 m). Too flat → solids settle and block; dips (bellies) collect sludge. Use a spirit level while fixing clamps.

steps.title: Things that block drains
steps.body: Cooking oil and ghee (solidifies), tea leaves, rice, hair, wet wipes, sanitary pads, cotton buds, plastic, construction debris. Toilets should receive only human waste and toilet paper. Educating customers prevents repeat calls.

lessons.title: Working as a plumber: estimates and customers

scenes.text: In Bhopal, Farhan and Joseph both quote for a bathroom pipe replacement.
Farhan says 'around four–five thousand, see as we go'. Joseph writes a list: materials, labour, time, and what is not included (tiles).
The customer chooses Joseph even though he is slightly more expensive. 'I know exactly what I'm paying for.'
Joseph finishes on time, cleans up and leaves a photo record of the concealed pipes. He gets three referrals.

steps.title: How to build a simple estimate
steps.body:
Break the job into lines:

- **Materials**: pipe length + 10% wastage, fittings (elbows, tees, unions, valves), solvent cement, tape, clamps.
- **Labour**: hours × rate (or a fixed rate per point/fitting, as is common locally).
- **Extras**: chiselling and patching walls, tile removal, debris disposal, transport.
- **Exclusions**: say clearly what is not included.
- **Validity**: e.g. 'valid for 15 days' as prices change.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Replacing 12 m of CPVC with 10 fittings:

- Pipe: 12 m + 10% = 13.2 m → buy enough standard lengths to cover it
- Fittings and cement: listed with shop prices
- Labour: 1 plumber + 1 helper, 1 day
- Wall chasing and patching: separate line

Total = materials + labour + extras. Add a small contingency (5–10%) for surprises and **tell the customer** it is there.

steps.title: Customer trust
steps.body:
- Show the old damaged part; explain the cause.
- Take **photos of concealed pipes** before tiling — future repairs become easy.
- Pressure-test new lines before closing walls.
- Give a simple warranty on your workmanship and honour it.
- Accept UPI/receipts and keep records.

steps.body: Plumber trades are offered at ITIs and as short-term skill courses through national skilling schemes and sector skill councils. scenes.text: Rekha in Mumbai got new kitchen cabinets. Within one monsoon the sink cabinet's base swelled and crumbled.
Carpenter Imran inspected it: 'This is ordinary particle board under the sink. Water and this board are enemies.'
He rebuilt it with waterproof-grade plywood and sealed edges with edge-banding.
Two monsoons later it was perfect. Rekha learned: the board matters as much as the design.

steps.title: Solid wood
steps.body:
Commonly used Indian timbers include **teak (sagwan)** — durable, stable, naturally resists termites and moisture, expensive; **sal** — very strong, used for door frames and structural work; **sheesham (Indian rosewood)** — hard, attractive grain, used for furniture; **mango wood** and **rubberwood** — affordable furniture woods that need proper seasoning/treatment.

Wood moves with humidity: it expands and shrinks across the grain much more than along it. Well-**seasoned** (dried) wood moves less and cracks less.

steps.title: Engineered boards
steps.body:
- **Plywood**: thin veneers glued in alternating grain directions — strong and stable. Grades you will hear: **MR** (moisture resistant, for dry interiors like wardrobes), **BWR** (boiling-water resistant) and **BWP / marine** (boiling-water proof, for kitchens, bathrooms, damp areas). Check for the relevant IS marking on the sheet.
- **Blockboard**: wooden strips core with veneer faces — good for long shelves and doors that shouldn't sag.
- **MDF**: smooth, paints well, good for shutters and CNC designs; swells badly if wet; holds screws poorly at edges.
- **Particle board**: cheapest; for low-cost dry-area furniture only.

Standard sheet size in India: **8 ft × 4 ft** (about 2440 × 1220 mm). Common thicknesses: 6, 9, 12, 18/19 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Particle board or MR ply under a sink or in a bathroom.
- Leaving board edges unsealed (water enters through edges first).
- Using unseasoned wood — doors warp and joints open.
- Ignoring termites: treat wood, keep it off damp walls, inspect regularly.

steps.title: Worked example: choosing materials for a kitchen
steps.body:
- Carcass under sink: **BWP / marine ply**, edges banded, with a water-resistant laminate.
- Wall cabinets: BWR ply is commonly used.
- Shutters: BWP ply or good-quality boards with laminate/acrylic.
- Shelves over 90 cm long: 18/19 mm ply or blockboard, or add a middle support to prevent sag.

story.title: The 2 mm that ruined a drawer

scenes.text: Apprentice Karan in Ludhiana cut eight drawer sides, each measured from the previous piece.
The small errors added up; the last drawer was 6 mm short and wobbled.
Master carpenter Gurdeep ji showed him: mark all pieces from one reference edge, use a stop block, and cut on the waste side of the line.
The next set fit perfectly. 'Accuracy is a habit, not luck,' said Gurdeep ji.

steps.title: Measuring and marking tools
steps.body:
- **Measuring tape** (metric and imperial) and **steel rule**.
- **Try square** — checks and marks 90°.
- **Combination square / sliding bevel** — 45° and other angles.
- **Marking gauge** — scratches a line parallel to an edge.
- **Sharp pencil or marking knife** — a thick pencil line can be 1 mm wide!

Units: 1 inch = **25.4 mm**; 1 foot = 12 inches = **304.8 mm**. Pick one system per project to avoid conversion errors.

steps.title: Good marking habits
steps.body:
- Choose a straight **reference edge** and square end; measure everything from it.
- Mark with a 'V' or tick to show the exact point, not a blob.
- Mark the **waste side** with an X and cut on that side of the line — the saw blade itself removes 2–3 mm (the **kerf**).
- For identical parts, use a **stop block** or cut them together.
- Check diagonals of a frame: if both diagonals are equal, it is square.

steps.title: Worked example: cutting list from an 8 × 4 sheet
steps.body:
You need shelves 600 mm × 300 mm from a 2440 × 1220 mm sheet, with a 3 mm kerf.

- Across the 1220 mm width: 300 + 3 + 300 + 3 + 300 + 3 + 300 = 1209 mm → **4 strips** fit (11 mm left).
- Along 2440 mm: 600 + 3 + 600 + 3 + 600 + 3 + 600 = 2409 mm → **4 pieces** per strip.
- Total = 4 × 4 = **16 shelves** from one sheet.

Forgetting kerf is the most common planning mistake — 600 × 4 = 2400 looks like it fits, but each cut eats wood.

steps.title: Check diagonals: the carpenter's square test
steps.body: For a rectangle 900 mm × 1200 mm, the diagonal should be √(900² + 1200²) = **1500 mm** (a 3-4-5 triangle scaled up). Measure both diagonals; adjust until they match. This works for doors, frames and even room layouts.

steps.title: Hand tools every carpenter uses
steps.body:
- **Saws**: rip saw (along the grain), crosscut saw (across the grain), tenon/back saw for joints, coping saw for curves.
- **Chisels** for joints and cleaning corners; keep them sharp — a blunt chisel slips.
- **Planes** to flatten and smooth.
- **Hammer, mallet, screwdrivers, clamps**, and a **drill** with wood bits.

Keep tools sharp, clean and stored; a sharp tool needs less force and is safer.

steps.title: Power tools
steps.body:
- **Circular saw / table saw** for straight cuts; **jigsaw** for curves; **router** for edges and grooves; **drill-driver**; **orbital sander**.

Before use: check the cable and plug, blade condition and guard; clamp the work; unplug before changing blades or bits.

steps.title: Safety rules that save fingers and eyes
steps.body:
- **Eye protection** always; **ear protection** for saws and routers; **dust mask** for sanding, MDF dust especially.
- No loose sleeves, gloves near spinning blades (they can be pulled in), or dangling jewellery; tie long hair.
- Use **push sticks** for narrow cuts; never reach over a running blade.
- Keep guards and riving knives fitted.
- Wait for the blade to stop fully.
- Keep the floor clear of offcuts and cables.

steps.title: Screws, nails and pilot holes
steps.body:
- Drill a **pilot hole** before screwing into hardwood or near edges to prevent splitting.
- Countersink so screw heads sit flush.
- Nails hold well against sideways loads but can pull out; screws resist pull-out; glue + screws is strongest for furniture.
- In board edges, use screws designed for boards and keep away from the very edge.

steps.title: Common joints
steps.body:
- **Butt joint**: two pieces meet end-to-face; weakest; needs screws, dowels or brackets.
- **Lap / halving joint**: each piece cut half-depth — frames.
- **Dado / housing**: groove holds a shelf — strong for bookshelves.
- **Rebate (rabbet)**: step along an edge — cabinet backs.
- **Dowel joint**: wooden pins + glue — simple and strong when aligned.
- **Mortise and tenon**: tongue fits a slot — chairs, tables, doors; very strong.
- **Dovetail**: interlocking — drawer corners; resists pulling apart.

steps.title: Gluing well
steps.body:
- Use the right adhesive: PVA/synthetic resin wood glue for interiors; waterproof adhesives for wet areas.
- Surfaces must be clean, flat and fit well — glue doesn't fill big gaps.
- **Clamp** with even pressure, check square, wipe squeeze-out with a damp cloth before it dries.
- Respect the drying/curing time on the label before loading the joint.

steps.title: Sanding and finishing
steps.body:
- Sand **with the grain**, going through grits: e.g. **80 → 120 → 180 → 220**. Don't skip more than one step; each grit removes the scratches of the previous.
- Remove dust before finishing.
- Finishes: **wood stain** (colour), **melamine** and **PU (polyurethane)** polishes (durable, common in India), **French polish** (traditional shellac, beautiful but less water-resistant), **laminates and veneers** for boards, paint for MDF.
- Apply thin coats; sand lightly with fine grit between coats.

steps.title: Finishing safety
steps.body: Solvents and polishes are flammable and their fumes harmful: ventilate, avoid sparks and smoking, wear a suitable mask and gloves. **Oily rags can self-heat and catch fire** — spread them flat outdoors to dry or soak in water before disposal.

Keep a portfolio of before/after photos, give written estimates, and learn design basics and customer communication — they lift income as much as skill does.

lessons.title: How cooling works

story.title: Why the outdoor unit is hot

scenes.text: In Nagpur's May heat, 12-year-old Tanvi touched the AC's outdoor unit and pulled her hand back. 'It's making cold — why is it hot?'
Technician Prakash smiled: 'The AC doesn't make cold. It carries heat out of your room and dumps it outside.'
He drew a loop: compressor → condenser → expansion valve → evaporator → back to compressor.
Tanvi's father, Sameer, realised why the outdoor unit must never be boxed in.

steps.title: The refrigeration cycle
steps.body:
A refrigerant circulates in a sealed loop:

1. **Compressor** squeezes refrigerant gas → it becomes hot, high-pressure gas.
2. **Condenser** (outdoor coil + fan) releases that heat outside → refrigerant turns into a high-pressure liquid.
3. **Expansion device** (capillary tube or expansion valve) drops the pressure suddenly → refrigerant becomes very cold.
4. **Evaporator** (indoor coil) absorbs heat from room air blown over it → refrigerant boils back into gas; room air becomes cooler and drier.

The same principle runs your fridge: the coil at the back or the warm sides are its condenser.

steps.title: Tons, BTU and star labels
steps.body:
- **1 ton of refrigeration = 12,000 BTU/hour ≈ 3.5 kW of cooling** — it describes heat removed, not weight.
- A rough guide many dealers use: about 1 ton for a small room (~100–120 sq ft), 1.5 ton for a medium room, 2 ton for larger rooms — but sun exposure, top floor, number of people and windows change this.
- The **BEE star label** shows energy efficiency; for ACs it uses **ISEER** (Indian Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio). More stars = less electricity for the same cooling. Star thresholds are revised periodically, so compare labels of the same year.
- **Inverter ACs** vary compressor speed instead of switching fully on/off — usually saving energy at part load.

steps.title: Why 24 °C
steps.body: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency recommends a default setting of about **24 °C**. Each degree higher saves energy (BEE has cited roughly 6% per degree). Combine with a ceiling fan — moving air makes 26 °C feel much cooler. Close curtains in the afternoon and seal door gaps.

steps.title: Refrigerants need trained hands
steps.body:
Refrigerants such as R-32, R-410A and R-290 are under pressure; some (R-32 mildly, R-290 highly) are **flammable**, and older R-22 is being phased out because it harms the ozone layer. Venting gas harms the environment. Gas charging, brazing and leak repair are for trained, equipped technicians.

A sealed system should not need regular 'gas top-ups' — **if gas is low, there is a leak** that must be found and fixed.

scenes.text: In Kolkata, water dripped from Dr. Roy's bedroom AC onto the bed.
Technician Shabnam switched off and unplugged, opened the front panel: filters thick with dust, the coil iced, the drain tray full.
She washed the filters, cleared the drain pipe and checked the slope of the pipe.
Cooling improved immediately. 'Most AC complaints are dirty filters and blocked drains,' she said.

steps.title: User-level care (anyone can do this)
steps.body:
- **Switch off and unplug / switch off the MCB** first.
- **Clean filters every 2 weeks** in heavy use: slide out, wash with plain water, dry in shade, refit.
- Keep the **outdoor unit** in the open with clear airflow; don't cover it while running; remove leaves and nests.
- Keep doors and windows closed while running.
- Book a **professional service** (coil cleaning, drain flushing, checks) before summer and as the manual suggests.

steps.title: Symptom → likely cause
steps.body:
- **Water dripping indoors** → blocked drain pipe, dirty filter causing ice, or poor drain slope.
- **Ice on indoor pipes** → dirty filter, low airflow or low refrigerant (leak).
- **Weak cooling** → dirty filters/coils, outdoor unit in hot enclosed space, wrong tonnage, low gas.
- **Outdoor fan runs, compressor doesn't** → often a failed capacitor, compressor protection, or supply issue (technician job).
- **Error code** on display → note it and check the manual; technicians use it to diagnose.

steps.title: Hidden dangers inside appliances
steps.body:
- **Capacitors** in AC outdoor units and motors can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged — trained technicians discharge them safely before touching.
- Outdoor units on high walls need **fall protection** — many technician injuries are falls.
- ACs usually need a dedicated **16 A circuit** with proper earthing; never run them from extension boards.

steps.title: Saving money on AC bills
steps.body: Set 24–26 °C with a fan, use sleep/eco mode, keep filters clean, shade the outdoor unit from direct afternoon sun without blocking airflow, and choose higher-star inverter models when buying. Units saved per year often pay back the extra cost of an efficient model within a few years.

Next, a washing machine that won't drain — the drain filter is full of coins and hair.
Last, a geyser that hisses and drips from a small valve. 'That's the safety valve doing its job — the thermostat has failed.'
Ravi notes: two of three problems were user-fixable. He shows each customer what to check next time.

steps.title: Refrigerator
steps.body:
- Keep the fridge at about **3–5 °C** and freezer at about **−18 °C** for food safety.
- Leave a gap (as per manual, often a few cm) behind and at the sides for the condenser to release heat.
- Don't overfill — cold air must circulate.
- Check door gaskets: close the door on a paper strip; if it slides out easily, the seal leaks.
- Frost-free models defrost automatically; direct-cool models need manual defrosting when ice builds up.

steps.title: Washing machine
steps.body:
- Install **level** on a firm floor; unlevel machines vibrate and 'walk'.
- Clean the **drain/pump filter** (front-loaders, usually behind a small door at the bottom) and the lint filter regularly.
- Wipe the **door gasket** and leave the door open after use to stop mould.
- Use the right amount of detergent — too much causes residue and smells.
- Proper **earthing** is essential: a machine that tingles has a fault.

steps.title: Geyser (water heater)
steps.body:
- **Thermostat** controls temperature; the **safety / pressure-relief valve** releases pressure if it rises dangerously — it must never be blocked or plugged.
- In hard-water areas, scale builds up on the element; the **anode rod** (in many storage geysers) protects the tank and wears out over time.
- Geysers need a **16 A circuit, good earthing and an RCCB**. Many electricians also advise switching the geyser off before bathing.
- Signs to stop and call a technician: tingling from taps, scalding water, constant dripping from the valve, burning smell.

steps.title: Unplug first, always
steps.body: Before cleaning any appliance filter or gasket: switch off and unplug. Never open covers that need tools — motors, heaters, capacitors and wiring are inside. Never bypass a geyser's thermostat or safety valve.

steps.title: Try this

The repair costs a fraction of a compressor. The customer becomes her best referrer.

steps.title: A structured diagnosis
steps.body:
1. **Listen**: symptoms, when it started, sounds, smells, error codes, recent events (power cut, shifting).
2. **Check supply**: socket, plug, voltage, MCB/RCCB.
3. **Look and feel (safely)**: airflow, ice patterns, fan running, heat at condenser.
4. **Use the error code and service manual**.
5. **Test components** with the right meter (trained technicians only for live tests).
6. **Repair the root cause**, test fully, explain to the customer.

steps.title: Business basics
steps.body:
- Price clearly: visit charge + labour + parts; show old parts.
- Use genuine/quality parts; give a warranty on your work.
- Keep a service record per customer — remind them before summer (AC) or after a year (servicing).
- Use online listings carefully and maintain good reviews.
- Behave professionally inside homes: shoe covers, ID, explain before acting.

steps.title: Training
steps.body: Common routes: the ITI trade **Refrigeration and Air-Conditioning Technician**, short-term skilling courses, and manufacturer/brand service training. Refrigerant handling and brazing need hands-on supervised training with proper equipment; growing areas include inverter electronics, VRF systems in offices, and heat-pump water heaters.

steps.title: Refuse unsafe shortcuts
steps.body:
- Never bypass thermostats, overload protectors or safety valves.
- Never vent refrigerant deliberately.
- Never work at height without proper support; outdoor AC units on high walls need safe access.
- If you are not trained for a job, refer it — reputation lasts longer than one job's fee.

scenes.text: Aman, 17, in Patna is saving for his first scooter. His uncle Rajesh runs a two-wheeler workshop.
Rajesh opens an old engine on the bench: piston, valves, spark plug. 'Four strokes,' he says. 'Mechanics remember them as suck, squeeze, bang, blow.'
Then he shows an electric scooter: battery, controller, hub motor — no oil change, no spark plug.
Aman decides to learn both. 'The future workshop needs both,' says Rajesh.

steps.title: The four-stroke petrol engine
steps.body:
1. **Intake**: piston moves down, intake valve opens, air–fuel mixture enters.
2. **Compression**: valves closed, piston moves up and squeezes the mixture.
3. **Power**: the **spark plug** fires; burning gas pushes the piston down — this is the work stroke.
4. **Exhaust**: piston moves up, exhaust valve opens, burnt gases leave.

The crankshaft turns the up-and-down motion into rotation → gearbox → wheels (via chain or belt in two-wheelers). **Diesel engines** have no spark plug: they compress air so much that injected fuel ignites from the heat (compression ignition).

steps.title: Electric vehicles
steps.body:
EVs use a **battery pack**, a **controller** and an **electric motor**. No engine oil, spark plugs or clutch; regenerative braking returns some energy to the battery. They still need **tyres, brakes, suspension, lights, coolant (in many cars for battery/motor cooling) and software updates**.

Safety: EV high-voltage systems (orange cables in cars) are only for trained technicians.

steps.title: Fluids and what they do
steps.body:
- **Engine oil**: lubricates, cools and cleans moving parts.
- **Coolant** (in liquid-cooled engines): carries heat to the radiator. Many small motorcycles and scooters are air-cooled.
- **Brake fluid** (hydraulic brakes): transmits lever/pedal force; absorbs moisture over time, so it is replaced at intervals.
- **Gear oil / transmission fluid**, **washer fluid**.

Use the grade specified in the **owner's manual** — the single most useful document for your vehicle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the wrong oil grade or 'any oil'.
- Ignoring service intervals in the manual.
- Overfilling oil above MAX (can damage seals).
- Continuing to drive after a red warning light comes on.

scenes.text: Fatima drives from Pune to Mumbai every Friday. Her car felt heavy and used more fuel.
At a petrol pump, attendant Dinesh checked: front tyres were 22 psi; the door sticker said 33.
After correcting pressure, the steering felt light and her fuel efficiency improved.
Fatima now does a five-minute check every Sunday morning.

steps.title: Tyres
steps.body:
- Check pressure **when tyres are cold** (before driving far), using the figure on the **door-jamb sticker, fuel flap or owner's manual** — not the maximum printed on the tyre sidewall.
- Under-inflation → heavier steering, more fuel, overheating, blowouts. Over-inflation → less grip, harsh ride.
- Check **tread**: small raised bars in the grooves are **tread-wear indicators**; when the tread is level with them, replace the tyre.
- Look for cuts, bulges, nails. Don't forget the spare.

steps.title: Oil, coolant and fluids
steps.body:
- **Engine oil**: on level ground, engine off for a few minutes. Pull the dipstick, wipe, reinsert fully, pull again — level should be between MIN and MAX. Many scooters have a dipstick on the oil filler cap; some motorcycles have a sight glass.
- **Coolant**: check the reservoir level against marks **only when the engine is cold**. **Never open a hot radiator cap** — scalding coolant can spray out.
- **Brake fluid**: reservoir between marks; a sudden drop suggests a leak or worn pads.
- **Washer fluid**: top up with water and a suitable washer additive.

steps.title: Lights, horn, wipers, brakes
steps.body: Walk around with someone: headlights (low/high), indicators, brake lights, reverse light, hazard lights, horn, wipers. Test brakes gently at low speed before a journey. A brake pedal or lever that feels spongy or travels too far needs immediate checking.

One evening the rusty, loose chain jumped off the sprocket in traffic. He wasn't hurt, but lost a day's earnings.
Mechanic Salma showed him how to check slack, clean and lubricate the chain, and how worn sprockets look like shark teeth.
Sandeep now lubes his chain every weekend and his chain set lasts much longer.

steps.title: Chain and sprockets (motorcycles)
steps.body:
- **Slack**: with the bike on its stand and engine off, push the chain up and down at the midpoint of the lower run. Many motorcycles specify around **20–30 mm** of free play — **check your manual**.
- Too tight → strains bearings and the chain; too loose → can jump off.
- **Clean and lubricate** with chain lube regularly (commonly every few hundred km, and after rain or washing).
- Replace chain and sprockets together when sprocket teeth look hooked or the chain has tight spots.
- Scooters usually use a **CVT belt** inside a cover — replaced at service intervals.

steps.title: Brakes
steps.body:
- **Drum brakes**: check free play of the lever/pedal and adjust as per manual; many drums have a wear indicator.
- **Disc brakes**: check pad thickness through the caliper and brake fluid level.
- Many newer two-wheelers have **CBS** (combined braking) or **ABS**. Practise braking smoothly with both brakes.
- Squealing, grinding or a spongy lever → get it checked immediately.

steps.title: Battery, spark plug and air filter
steps.body:
- Keep battery terminals clean and tight; slow cranking or a weak horn suggests a weak battery.
- The spark plug and air filter are checked/cleaned/replaced at service intervals; a clogged air filter reduces mileage, especially in dusty conditions.
- Engine oil changes follow the manual's kilometre or time interval, whichever comes first.

steps.title: Safety while maintaining
steps.body: Engine and exhaust get very hot — let them cool. Keep fingers away from chain and sprocket; never check the chain with the engine running or the wheel turning under power. Petrol is highly flammable: no smoking, no flames.

steps.title: Dashboard warning-light colours
steps.body:
- **Red** = serious, stop safely as soon as possible: oil pressure, engine temperature, brake system, battery/charging, airbag.
- **Amber/yellow** = check soon, drive carefully: check-engine light, ABS, tyre pressure (TPMS), low fuel.
- **Green/blue** = information: headlights, high beam, indicators, cruise control.

The owner's manual explains each symbol for your model.

steps.title: If the engine overheats
steps.body:
1. Turn off the AC; if safe, turn the heater to full to pull heat from the engine.
2. Pull over safely, hazard lights on, switch off the engine.
3. **Don't open the radiator cap** while hot.
4. Once fully cool, check coolant level and look for leaks.
5. Call roadside assistance if unsure. Driving on with an overheating engine can destroy it.

steps.title: Changing a flat tyre on a car — step by step
steps.body:
1. Stop on flat, firm ground well away from traffic; hazard lights on; handbrake on; passengers out to a safe place.
2. Place a warning triangle behind the car if you have one; wedge the diagonally opposite wheel.
3. **Loosen** wheel nuts slightly while the wheel is on the ground.
4. Place the jack at the **jacking point** shown in the manual; raise until the tyre clears the ground. Never put any body part under a car on a jack.
5. Remove nuts, swap wheel, hand-tighten nuts.
6. Lower the car; tighten nuts in a **criss-cross (star) pattern**.
7. Check spare pressure; re-check nut tightness after a short distance; get the flat repaired soon.

steps.title: Breakdowns and accidents
steps.body:
- Move to safety first; on highways stand away from traffic, behind barriers if possible.
- Call **112** for emergencies; most insurers and manufacturers offer roadside assistance — save the number in your phone.
- In India, the law protects **Good Samaritans** who help accident victims in good faith: they cannot be harassed or forced to give personal details.

She learns a trick from her driving instructor, Harpreet ji: 'Circles order you. Triangles warn you. Rectangles inform you.'

steps.title: Mandatory (regulatory) signs — mostly circles
steps.body:
These are **orders**. Disobeying them is an offence.

- **Red circle** = prohibition: No entry (red circle with a white horizontal bar), No U-turn, No overtaking, No parking (blue circle with red border and a red diagonal), No stopping or standing (red cross on blue), Horn prohibited, Speed limit (number in a red circle), height/weight/width limits.
- **Blue circle** = compulsory action: Compulsory turn left, Compulsory keep left, Compulsory cycle track, Compulsory sound horn.
- Two special shapes: **STOP** is a red **octagon** — come to a complete stop. **GIVE WAY** is a red-bordered **inverted triangle** — slow down and give priority.

steps.title: Cautionary (warning) signs — red-bordered triangles pointing up
steps.body: These **warn** of hazards ahead so you can slow down and be ready: school ahead, pedestrian crossing, men at work, sharp bend left/right, hairpin bend, narrow road/bridge, speed breaker, slippery road, cattle, falling rocks, guarded/unguarded railway crossing, cross road, side road, roundabout ahead, steep ascent/descent, gap in median.

steps.title: Informatory signs — rectangles
steps.body: These **guide and inform**: hospital, first aid post, petrol pump, parking (white P on blue), eating place, light refreshment, rest house, destination and distance boards (often **green on national highways**, blue on other roads), park this side.

steps.title: Memory trick and road markings
steps.body:
**Circles command, triangles warn, rectangles inform.**

Road markings matter too: a **continuous (solid) centre line** — do not cross or overtake across it; **broken line** — you may cross when safe; **double solid** — never cross; **zebra crossing** — pedestrians have priority; **stop line** — stop behind it at signals.

scenes.text: Kabir, a new driver in Bengaluru, freezes at a busy roundabout. Horns blare.
His instructor Deepa explains: 'Traffic already on the roundabout has priority. We go clockwise, keep left, and signal before we exit.'
At the next junction she shows him the stop line, the amber light, and why he must wait for pedestrians on the zebra crossing.
By the end of the week, Kabir drives through rush hour calmly.

steps.title: Keep left, overtake from the right
steps.body: India drives on the **left**. Keep to the left side of the road, letting faster vehicles pass on your right. **Overtake only from the right**, when the road ahead is clear and visible — never on bends, bridges, pedestrian crossings, near junctions or across a solid centre line. Do not speed up when someone is overtaking you.

steps.title: Right of way
steps.body:
- At an **uncontrolled junction of equal roads**, give way to traffic approaching from your **right**.
- Traffic on a **main road** has priority over traffic entering from a side road.
- At **roundabouts**, give way to traffic already on the roundabout; circulate **clockwise**.
- **Pedestrians** on zebra crossings have priority.
- **Ambulances, fire engines and police vehicles** on emergency duty: move aside and give way — obstructing them is an offence.

steps.title: Signals and lanes
steps.body:
- **Red**: stop behind the stop line. **Amber**: stop if you safely can; don't race it. **Green**: go if the junction is clear. **Flashing amber**: proceed with caution. **Flashing red**: stop, then proceed when safe.
- Use **indicators** well before turning or changing lanes; check mirrors and blind spot (**mirror–signal–manoeuvre**).
- On multi-lane roads, keep to your lane; use the right lane for overtaking, not cruising.
- Use **dipped headlights** in the city and when facing oncoming traffic; don't dazzle others with high beam.

steps.title: Common mistakes new drivers make
steps.body: Wrong-side driving to save a U-turn, overtaking from the left, stopping on zebra crossings, honking unnecessarily (and in silence zones near hospitals and schools), parking on footpaths, not signalling, and following too closely.

scenes.text: Vishal and his friend Neha are stopped at a traffic checkpoint in Hyderabad.
Vishal shows his DL, RC, insurance and PUC on DigiLocker. Neha's pillion helmet is in her hand, not on her head.
The officer explains that pillion riders must wear helmets too, and issues a challan.
Neha buys her own ISI-marked helmet the same day.

steps.title: Learner's licence → driving licence
steps.body:
- **Age**: 16 for a gearless two-wheeler up to 50 cc (with parent/guardian consent); **18** for other motor vehicles such as cars and geared motorcycles.
- **Learner's licence (LL)**: apply through the official Parivahan Sarathi portal or RTO; there is a test on road signs and rules (many states offer it online). An LL is valid for **6 months**. While learning a car, display 'L' plates and drive only with a licensed driver beside you.
- **Driving licence (DL)**: you can take the driving test **after 30 days** from issue of the LL (and before it expires).
- Always check your state RTO's current procedure and fees.

steps.title: Documents you must carry
steps.body:
- **Driving licence**
- **Registration certificate (RC)**
- **Insurance** — at least **third-party insurance is compulsory**
- **PUC** (Pollution Under Control) certificate

Digital copies in **DigiLocker or mParivahan** are accepted as valid.

steps.title: Key laws (Motor Vehicles Act, as amended in 2019)
steps.body:
- **Helmets**: rider and pillion must wear a properly fastened, BIS-certified helmet (a limited exemption exists for Sikhs wearing a turban).
- **Seat belts**: for all occupants, front and rear.
- **Drink-driving**: the limit is **30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood**; penalties include heavy fines and imprisonment. The safest rule: if you drink, don't drive.
- **Mobile phones**: using a handheld phone while driving is an offence.
- **Juvenile driving**: if a minor commits a traffic offence, the guardian or vehicle owner can be held liable, the vehicle's registration can be cancelled, and the minor can be barred from getting a licence until a later age.
- Fines were raised sharply in 2019 and amounts can vary by state — check official state transport sites.

steps.title: Good Samaritan protection
steps.body: A person who helps an accident victim in good faith is protected from civil and criminal liability and cannot be forced to share personal details. Call **112**, give first aid if trained, and help get the victim to hospital — quick help in the first hour after a crash saves lives.

steps.title: Important note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Rules, fines and procedures change and vary by state — always check the official Parivahan portal and your state transport department.

scenes.text: On a rainy evening on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway, Ananya kept a long gap behind a truck.
The truck braked suddenly for a stalled car. Ananya had time to slow smoothly; a tailgating car beside her swerved dangerously.
Her father, a bus driver for 25 years, had taught her: 'Expect the mistakes of others. Space is your safety.'
She arrives home safely and teaches her younger cousin the three-second rule.

steps.title: Keep a safe following distance
steps.body:
Pick a fixed object (a pole or sign). When the vehicle ahead passes it, count 'one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three'. If you reach the object before finishing, you're too close.

- **At least 3 seconds** in good conditions.
- **Double it** in rain, fog, at night or behind heavy vehicles.
- Braking distance grows roughly with the **square of speed**: double the speed ≈ four times the braking distance.

steps.title: See, predict, act
steps.body:
- **Look far ahead**, not just at the vehicle in front.
- **Check mirrors** every few seconds and before braking or turning.
- Watch for **vulnerable road users**: pedestrians, cyclists, children, animals.
- **Blind spots**: big vehicles can't see you beside or close behind them — if you can't see the driver's mirrors, they can't see you.
- Never drive tired: take breaks about every two hours on long drives.

steps.title: Rain, fog and night
steps.body:
- Slow down; use dipped headlights (and fog lamps if fitted) in fog, not high beam.
- Avoid sudden braking or steering on wet roads; on waterlogged roads, if you can't see the road surface, don't enter.
- If the vehicle skids, ease off the accelerator and steer gently where you want to go.

steps.title: At an accident scene
steps.body:
1. Park safely ahead, hazards on.
2. Protect the scene; watch traffic.
3. Call **112** with the exact location (landmarks, km stone).
4. Don't move injured people unless there's immediate danger (fire, traffic) — spinal injury risk.
5. If trained, give first aid: check breathing, control bleeding with firm pressure.
6. Stay calm; you're protected as a Good Samaritan.

courses.summary: Lay out a shop that sells, manage stock and margins with real numbers, serve customers and take digital payments safely, and keep simple daily accounts including credit.

scenes.text: Ramu's kirana store in Mysuru was crowded and dark; customers asked for items and waited while he searched.
His daughter Kavya, a commerce student, suggested better lighting, grouped categories, and price labels.
They placed small impulse items (chocolates, batteries) near the billing counter and essentials where customers walk past other goods.
Within two months, average bill size rose and customers found things themselves.

steps.title: Layout principles
steps.body:
- **Group by category** (staples, snacks, personal care, cleaning) so customers can find things.
- **Essentials deeper inside** — customers walking to buy rice or milk pass other products.
- **Impulse items near billing** — chocolates, gum, small batteries, phone accessories.
- **Clear aisles** and good lighting; nothing blocking the entrance.
- **Price labels** on shelves or products — customers trust visible prices.

steps.title: Display and merchandising
steps.body:
- **Eye level is buy level**: put high-margin or featured items at eye level; kids' items lower.
- **Face products forward** and keep shelves full — empty shelves look like a closing shop.
- **Seasonal displays**: festival items, school supplies in June, umbrellas before monsoon.
- **Clean and dust daily** — a dusty product looks old.

steps.title: FIFO and FEFO
steps.body: Rotate stock so older items sell first: **FIFO** (first in, first out) and, for perishables and medicines, **FEFO** (first expiry, first out). Put new stock at the back, older at the front. Check expiry dates weekly; remove expired goods — selling them harms customers and your reputation and can break the law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Overcrowded shelves, no prices, expired goods mixed with fresh, fast-moving items hidden, and a cluttered counter that slows billing.

scenes.text: Neha opened a stationery shop near a school in Bhopal. She bought pens at ₹8 and sold at ₹10, thinking she made 25%.
Her accountant uncle explained: 25% is markup on cost; her margin on sales is 20%.
He also showed her a reorder level, so she'd never run out of notebooks in June again.
Neha now plans prices using margin and never misses the school-reopening rush.

steps.title: Markup vs margin
steps.body:
- **Markup** = profit ÷ **cost** × 100.
- **Margin** = profit ÷ **selling price** × 100.

Example: cost ₹80, selling price ₹100, profit ₹20.

- Markup = 20 ÷ 80 = **25%**
- Margin = 20 ÷ 100 = **20%**

Confusing the two makes shopkeepers think they earn more than they do.

steps.title: Setting a price for a target margin
steps.body:
Selling price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin).

Cost ₹60, target margin 25%: 60 ÷ 0.75 = **₹80**. Check: profit ₹20 ÷ ₹80 = 25% ✔.

On packaged goods, you **cannot charge more than the printed MRP** — so your margin is set by your purchase price and the MRP.

steps.title: Reorder level and safety stock
steps.body:
**Reorder level = average daily sales × supplier lead time (days) + safety stock.**

Example: you sell 12 packets of biscuits a day, the distributor takes 3 days, and you keep 10 extra as safety: 12 × 3 + 10 = **46**. When stock falls to 46 packets, reorder.

Too much stock ties up cash and risks expiry; too little loses sales.

steps.title: Know your fast and slow movers
steps.body: Track weekly sales of your top items. Fast movers need reliable reordering; slow movers need less space, smaller orders or offers. A simple notebook or a free billing app can show this.

scenes.text: A young man at Farida's mobile accessories shop in Pune showed a 'payment successful' screen for ₹1,200 and walked off quickly.
Farida's soundbox hadn't announced anything. She checked her UPI app — no payment.
She learned: always confirm on your own soundbox or app, never the customer's screen.
She now politely waits for her own confirmation for every payment.

steps.title: Taking UPI payments safely
steps.body:
- Display your **own QR code**; check it hasn't been covered or replaced by someone else's.
- **Confirm on your own device** (soundbox, app notification or bank statement) — never trust the customer's screen or a screenshot.
- To **receive** money you never need to enter your UPI PIN. Anyone asking you to 'enter PIN to receive' or 'scan to receive' is scamming you.
- Never share OTPs or PINs with anyone, including callers claiming to be from the bank.
- Report cyber fraud quickly on **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in.

steps.title: Customer service that brings people back
steps.body:
- Greet customers; remember regulars' names and preferences.
- If an item is out of stock, offer an alternative or to order it.
- Handle complaints calmly: listen, apologise for the trouble, fix it (exchange/refund as per your policy), thank them.
- Offer home delivery or WhatsApp orders if practical.

steps.title: Consumer rules every shopkeeper should know
steps.body:
- Don't sell packaged goods **above MRP**; weights and measures must be accurate and scales verified as per Legal Metrology rules.
- Give a **bill/receipt** when asked; it builds trust.
- Don't sell expired or unsafe goods.
- Customers can raise complaints under the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, including through the **National Consumer Helpline (1915)**.
- **GST**: registration becomes mandatory above a turnover threshold — generally ₹40 lakh for goods suppliers (lower in some states) and ₹20 lakh for services (lower in some states). Check the GST portal or a tax professional for current rules.

This is general education, not legal or tax advice.

scenes.text: Gopal's grocery in Varanasi gave credit to many families. His notebook was messy; he forgot who owed what.
At year end, nearly ₹40,000 was stuck, and he had trouble paying his own suppliers.
His son set up a simple credit ledger app, a limit per customer, and polite monthly reminders.
Collections improved and Gopal could restock on time.

steps.title: The daily cash book
steps.body:
Every day, record:

- **Opening cash** (what's in the drawer at start)
- **Sales**: cash and UPI/card separately
- **Expenses**: purchases, electricity, wages, transport
- **Closing cash** (count it)

Opening + cash sales − cash expenses should equal closing cash. A mismatch means an error, a missed entry, or a loss — investigate the same day.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Opening cash ₹2,000. Cash sales ₹6,500. UPI sales ₹4,200 (goes to bank). Cash paid to supplier ₹3,000; tea and transport ₹200.

Expected closing cash = 2,000 + 6,500 − 3,000 − 200 = **₹5,300**.

Total sales for the day = 6,500 + 4,200 = **₹10,700**.

steps.title: Managing credit (udhaar) wisely
steps.body:
- Give credit only to known, regular customers.
- Set a **limit** per customer and a **due date** (e.g. monthly).
- Record every credit sale with date, items, amount — and get the customer to see or confirm it.
- Send polite reminders; many ledger apps send them automatically.
- Stop extra credit until old dues are cleared.
- Keep total credit within what your cash flow can handle.

steps.title: Know your monthly profit
steps.body: Monthly profit = total sales − cost of goods sold − expenses (rent, electricity, wages, transport, etc.). Separate your **personal spending** from the shop's money — mixing them is one of the most common reasons small shops struggle.

scenes.text: Aditi, a BCom student in Jaipur, made beautiful notes and slides for friends.
A senior suggested she offer presentation design to small businesses.
She chose a niche — pitch decks for startups and coaching institutes — and practised with three free samples.
Her first paid client came from a LinkedIn post. Six months later, she had steady weekend income.

steps.title: Skills people pay for online
steps.body:
- **Writing**: blogs, website copy, product descriptions, technical writing.
- **Design**: logos, social media posts, presentations, UI/UX.
- **Video and audio**: editing, subtitles, podcasts.
- **Development**: websites, apps, automation, data analysis.
- **Marketing**: social media management, SEO, ads.
- **Language**: translation, transcription, tutoring.
- **Support**: virtual assistance, bookkeeping, customer support.

steps.title: Choose a niche
steps.body: 'I do design' competes with millions. 'I design menus and Instagram posts for cafés' stands out. A niche = **skill × type of client × problem solved**. Start where you already have some skill or knowledge, and where clients can afford to pay.

steps.title: Getting good enough to be paid
steps.body:
- Practise on **real-looking projects**: redesign a local shop's menu, write blogs for an imaginary brand.
- Use free learning resources and practise daily.
- Ask for honest feedback from people in the field.
- Your first goal is not perfection — it's **reliable, on-time, clean** work.

steps.title: Watch out
steps.body: 'Data entry from home — earn ₹30,000 a week, pay ₹999 registration' is almost always a **scam**. Real clients pay you; you don't pay to get work.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your niche sentence: 'I help ___ (client type) with ___ (problem) by ___ (your skill).' Share it with a friend and ask if it's clear.

activity.prompt: List three skills you already have (even partly) and the kind of client who might pay for each. Which one excites you most, and why?

scenes.text: Rahul, a self-taught video editor in Guwahati, had no reviews on any platform.
He made three short before/after edits and wrote what problem each solved.
His profile headline changed from 'Video editor' to 'Short-form video editor for educators — captions, hooks, retention'.
A teacher with a YouTube channel hired him within two weeks.

steps.title: What a portfolio needs
steps.body:
- **3–6 best pieces**, not everything you've ever made.
- For each: the **problem**, what you did, and the **result** (e.g. 'reduced video length 40%, added captions').
- Before/after where possible.
- Only show work you're allowed to show; never use others' work as your own.
- Host it simply: a free website builder, Behance/Dribbble (design), GitHub (code), or a shared drive folder with a clean index.

steps.title: A profile that converts
steps.body:
- **Headline**: niche + benefit ('Website copy for Indian D2C brands that turns visitors into buyers').
- **Photo**: clear, friendly, professional.

scenes.text: Sameer, a designer in Indore, charged ₹200 per logo to win clients. He worked 14-hour days and still couldn't pay rent.

steps.title: Calculate your minimum rate
steps.body:
1. Monthly money you need (living + savings + taxes + software/internet).
2. Realistic **billable hours** per month — not all working hours are billable (admin, learning, finding clients). Many freelancers bill around half their working time.
3. **Minimum hourly rate = monthly need ÷ billable hours.**

Example: need ₹40,000/month, 80 billable hours → minimum **₹500/hour**.

steps.title: Hourly, project and package pricing
steps.body:
- **Hourly**: fair for unclear scope; clients may worry about cost.

- **Packages**: Basic / Standard / Premium — clients often choose the middle.

Always define **scope** (what's included), **revisions** (how many), and **timeline**.

steps.title: A proposal that wins

2. **Your approach**: 'I'll create a consistent look, plan a content calendar, and write captions.'
3. **Proof**: one relevant sample link.
4. **Options and price**, timeline, revisions.
5. **Clear next step**: 'Shall we start with a 15-minute call on Tuesday?'

Keep it short and specific — generic copy-paste proposals are ignored.
